title: Spec-Driven Development + MCP in Unreal
author: rdenubila
selftext:
Hey everyone, I wanted to share an experience I've been having with my game dev project, using AI to help me build it.

First of all, I think using MCP with Unreal is a one-way street. The latest version of the engine (5.8) already supports MCP natively, and everything points to this being the natural direction for the engine.

Game dev is a side thing for me. At my day job in software development we've been using SDD (Spec-Driven Development) for a while now, so I decided to try the same workflow on my games. It's been working really well.

Basically, before doing anything, the AI and I talk it through and agree on everything. It goes more or less like this:

First there's a file with the project rules, called the constitution. That's where the standards, the constraints and everything the AI learns along the way are kept.

Then I describe the feature I want and explain what it needs to do. The AI takes that and puts together an implementation plan, which I read carefully and adjust wherever I think it's needed.

Once the plan is settled, it breaks everything down into small tasks, and only after I approve the plan and the tasks does it actually start implementing, straight inside Unreal.

At the end I test it and check if it turned out the way I wanted.

Everything is saved in a folder inside the project itself, along with an [agent.md](http://agent.md) file that tells the AI how it should work.

The main advantages I see in using SDD:

* The AI keeps learning over time. Mistakes and problems found along the way get recorded and turned into rules for future implementations.
* Saving tokens: you can plan with a more expensive (and smarter) model and do the implementation with a cheaper one. Since the plan is already well defined, the simpler model can handle the implementation just fine.
* As the plan is being executed, each step gets validated and whatever's done gets saved in the document. So if you hit your daily token limit, you can pick it up with another agent or just wait for the limit to reset and keep going.
* The AI keeps the context of everything that was implemented before, so new features use that context naturally, without me having to rely on my memory or some other kind of documentation.
* The AI questions the implementation in ways I hadn't thought of. Many times I went to build a new feature for my game and, just by talking it through, the AI raised important points I hadn't considered.

Of course, even with the AI doing the implementation, there are still manual steps and you'll need to make plenty of adjustments. But using SDD with Unreal is the best way I've found so far to use AI as an ally in my development.

If you work with game dev and already use AI, I really recommend giving it a try. At first it feels a bit bureaucratic, but you quickly notice you spend a lot less time fixing things.

If you're interested and want to try it out, I made a repository with a base template you can add to your project. Here's the link:

[https://github.com/rdenubila/sdd-gamedev](https://github.com/rdenubila/sdd-gamedev)

comments.author: orellanaed
comments.body: Looks cool thanks for sharing, but FYI you left placeholder text in the License section: ***"Use it, fork it, adapt it. Add a license file (for example MIT) that suits how you want to share your version."***

comments.author: Ball_Analytics
comments.body:
1. I thought we already planned with the expensive model and implemented with the cheap one? 

2. How is this different from having ADRs and APIs that explains why decisions are made and what everything does respectively? 

3. Ive saved it so I’ll have a look when I get some time. And maybe answer my own questions.

replies.author: rdenubila
replies.body:
Thanks for the questions!

1. Yes, a lot of people already do that. The difference with SDD is that the plan becomes a document saved in the project, broken into small tasks. So the cheaper model follows something concrete, and if I hit a token limit, another agent can pick it up from the exact point where it stopped.
2. They're close, and they actually complement each other. ADRs and API docs explain decisions and what already exists. SDD is more about the workflow before building: spec, plan and tasks get reviewed and approved before any implementation starts. And the constitution works kind of like a living ADR that the AI reads every time, so past decisions turn into rules it follows automatically.
3. Awesome, hope it helps! Feel free to reach out if you have any questions when you try it.

replies.author: Ball_Analytics
replies.body: Might adopt, seems promising on my end, and I'll take anything that will make my work easier. :) appreciate the share.
